target.title: LipDiffuser: Lip-to-Speech Generation with Conditional Diffusion Models

read.pdf: Fig. 1, Fig. 2, Table 1 (as represented in text.txt)

entries.text: LipDiffuser synthesizes natural, intelligible speech from silent video and is configured with an enrollment voice embedding.
entries.condition: Inference uses silent video of the target speaker plus enrollment audio; the original input audio track is not required.

entries.text: The method uses MP-ADM as denoiser and introduces magnitude-preserving FiLM to fuse time-aligned video features.
entries.condition: Video features are interpolated to the audio-frame rate and fused in the denoiser decoder.
entries.quote:
We proposed
magnitude-preserving feature-wise linear modulation (MP-FiLM)
layers for feature fusion within the magnitude-preserving ablated
diffusion model (MP-ADM) network architecture.

entries.text: MP-FiLM is the authors' magnitude-preserving variant of FiLM, applied per frame so each lip movement conditions the corresponding audio frame.
entries.condition: Video conditioning is interpolated in time to the audio feature rate; learned video contribution is clamped between 0 and 1.
entries.quote:
Unlike the original FiLM, here the scaling and shifting of the
network’s activations are conducted per frame and not globally, so
that each lip movement conditions the corresponding audio frame.

entries.text: Training first uses audio-only pretraining; LRS3 training audio is enhanced before use.
entries.condition: Audio-only pretraining precedes visual conditioning; in-the-wild LRS3 audio is pre-enhanced with a pretrained Schrödinger-bridge speech-enhancement model.
entries.quote:
Therefore, we use a pretrained generative
SE model, specifically the Schr¨odinger bridge [27], [28], to enhance
the audio tracks of theLRS3dataset.

entries.text: A speaker embedding is extracted from an enrollment utterance of the target speaker; Table 1 says enrollment audio is from the clean reference.
entries.condition: Enrollment audio is required at inference; Table 1 uses enrollment derived from the clean reference.
entries.quote: Enrollment audio is derived from the clean reference.

entries.text: Inference uses a second-order deterministic diffusion sampler with 32 sampling steps.
entries.condition: Reverse diffusion generation of a mel-spectrogram, conditioned on precomputed video features and speaker embedding.
entries.quote:
We use the second-order deterministic sampler from [21]
withM= 32 sampling steps to generate a mel-spectrogramˆx∈Rna.

entries.text: The denoiser contains approximately 205 million parameters.
entries.condition: LipDiffuser denoiser model.

entries.text: Training runs for 32M samples with batch size 256 and peak learning rate 0.005.
entries.unit: training samples; examples/batch; peak learning rate
entries.condition: Linear learning-rate ramp-up followed by inverse-square-root decay; Adam optimizer; the paper does not state a seed or run count.

entries.text: Adam uses β1=0.9 and β2=0.99; the noise-level log-normal distribution uses Pmean=-1.2 and Pstd=1.2.
entries.condition: Training configuration for the proposed model; loss weighting follows the paper's stated time-dependent weighting and learned uncertainty projection.

entries.text: Audio-only pretraining uses 960 hours of LibriSpeech, also preprocessed by the speech-enhancement model.
entries.condition: Audio-only pretraining before video conditioning; data preprocessed by the pretrained generative speech-enhancement model.
entries.quote:
To increase the variety and quantity of
training data, we pretrain the model on the 960 hours of theLibriSpeech
dataset [31], also preprocessed by the SE model.

entries.text: LRS3-CHiME3 has six noise subsets at SNRs 5, 0, -5, -10, -15, and -20 dB.
entries.condition: Clean LRS3 speech mixed with randomly sampled CHiME3 noise files to the specified SNR for each subset.

entries.text: The in-domain LRS3-CHiME3 test set contains 1,321 files.
entries.condition: In-domain LRS3-CHiME3 test set; Table 1 evaluates systems at -10 dB SNR.
entries.quote:
We begin with in-domain results using theLRS3-CHiME3test set
comprising 1321 test files.

entries.text: Evaluation reports DNSMOS, NISQA, speaker cosine similarity, QuartzNet WER, phoneme similarity, and SyncNet lip-sync metrics.
entries.condition: WER uses QuartzNet15x5Base-En; LPS uses a w2v LV-60K phoneme predictor; SpkSim is cosine similarity; LSE-C/LSE-D use SyncNet.

entries.text: The formal listening experiment had 15 participants and used randomly selected LRS3-CHiME3 samples at -10 dB SNR.
entries.condition: Randomly selected LRS3-CHiME3 samples at -10 dB SNR; speech quality and speaker similarity only; sample count not stated.
entries.quote:
In addition to instrumental metrics, we also conducted a formal
listening experiment with 15 participants

entries.text: Listening ratings use a continuous 0-to-100 scale relative to a reference.
entries.condition: Ratings cover overall speech quality or speaker similarity compared to a reference.

entries.text: Authors claim LipDiffuser achieves the highest speech-quality scores and strongest speaker similarity among compared lip-to-speech systems.
entries.condition: In-domain LRS3-CHiME3 test results at -10 dB SNR, Table 1; quality metrics DNSMOS/NISQA and SpkSim.
entries.quote:
For lip-to-speech approaches, our
proposedLipDiffuserachieves the highest speech quality scores and
the strongest speaker similarity, approaching the clean reference.

entries.text: Authors characterize LipDiffuser, LipVoicer, and IL2S (SSL) as comparable on WER and LPS and substantially better than the speech-enhancement methods.
entries.condition: LRS3-CHiME3 in-domain test at -10 dB SNR; WER and LPS.
entries.quote:
In
terms of ASR performance,LipDiffuser,LipVoicer, andIL2S (SSL)
achieve comparable WER and LPS, all substantially outperforming
the SE methods.

entries.text: Authors claim lip-to-speech consistently outperforms speech enhancement below the -5 dB input-SNR threshold.
entries.condition: Figure 2 compares SGMSE+, AV-Gen, and LipDiffuser across input SNR; LipDiffuser does not use input audio.

entries.text: Authors claim cross-dataset evaluation shows generalization in speech quality and speaker similarity.
entries.condition: The text does not identify the cross-dataset evaluation dataset, test size, SNR, or speaker composition.
entries.quote:
Furthermore, cross-dataset evaluations demonstrate the strong
generalization capabilities of our method in both speech quality and
speaker similarity.

entries.text: Authors identify one-to-many viseme-to-phoneme mapping as a source of ambiguity in lip-to-speech.
entries.condition: Different phonemes may correspond to the same lip-movement sequence; the paper says longer temporal context can alleviate the issue.

entries.text: Authors identify visual/audio alignment as difficult because the modalities have very different feature rates.
entries.condition: The introduction gives video at 25 Hz and audio at 48 kHz as an example of the rate mismatch.

entries.text: The authors report that audio-only pretraining is required for the method to work.
entries.condition: Pretraining stage omits video conditioning features; then model is trained with paired audio-visual data.
entries.quote:
For the method to work, we
have found that an audio-only pretraining stage is required, without
video conditioning features.

entries.text: The audio input representation uses 16 kHz sampling, 1,024-point FFT, 256-sample hop, 62.5 Hz feature rate, and 80 mel bins; spectrograms are standardized to zero mean and variance 0.5 using training-set statistics.
entries.unit: Hz; FFT samples; hop samples; frames/s; mel bins; standardized mean; variance
entries.condition: Audio and mel representation used for training/evaluation; exact training-set statistics are not reported.

entries.text: Visual conditioning uses 25-fps grayscale mouth ROIs of 88×88 pixels and BRAVEn features of dimension 1,024 per video frame.
entries.condition: ROI extraction follows cited lipreading preprocessing; BRAVEn is the self-supervised video encoder.

entries.text: Wespeaker maps an enrollment utterance of arbitrary length to a 256-dimensional speaker embedding.
entries.condition: Speaker embedding is derived from the target speaker's enrollment audio.

entries.text: The generated mel-spectrogram is converted to waveform audio with a 16-kHz-pretrained HiFi-GAN decoder.
entries.condition: Waveform is synthesized after reverse diffusion from generated mel-spectrogram.

entries.text: Training on NVIDIA H100 GPUs typically requires 60 GPU-hours.
entries.condition: Training setup in Sec. 4; the text says typically and reports NVIDIA H100 hardware.

entries.text: Speech units are extracted from HuBERT-BASE SSL speech representations using K-means; the clustering model is trained on LJ Speech.
entries.condition: HuBERT-BASE SSL model; K-means training corpus is LJ Speech; units are an auxiliary target alongside mel-spectrogram.

entries.text: The speech-unit codebook has 200 clusters and units are sampled at 50 Hz.
entries.condition: For the L2S target; 20 ms of mel-spectrogram is stacked to match the unit sampling rate.

entries.text: Mel-spectrogram is predicted by a speaker-specific branch, while speech units are predicted by a speaker-agnostic branch; a speech-derived d-vector conditions the mel branch.
entries.condition: The speaker embedding is a d-vector extracted from a speech segment and provided to the speaker-specific predictor.

entries.text: The acoustic decoder is a HiFi-GAN-modified multi-input vocoder conditioned on mel-spectrogram, speech units, and speaker embedding; 128-D unit embeddings are upsampled to mel length and the speaker embedding is projected to 128-D and repeated.
entries.condition: Vocoder training augments mel input with blur and Gaussian noise to mimic predicted mel-spectrograms.

entries.text: LRS3 is a 433-hour sentence-level TED/TEDx audio-visual corpus with thousands of speakers; the split simulates an unseen-speaker test setting.
entries.condition: LRS3 test set; data splits follow prior work to simulate unseen speakers.

entries.text: Objective evaluation reports STOI, ESTOI, PESQ, and WER; STOI/ESTOI measure intelligibility, PESQ measures perceptual quality, and WER comes from pretrained speech recognition on generated speech.
entries.condition: Evaluated on each dataset's test set; the pretrained recognizer is trained on that dataset's audio; no decoding/LM or seed details are stated.

entries.text: DiffV2S uses an 8-layer, 4-head Transformer encoder (512 hidden, 1024 feed-forward) as denoiser; it conditions on channel-wise concatenation c=fv||sv of visual features and vision-guided speaker embeddings. Speaker embeddings are extracted from video by prompt-tuning a pretrained audio-visual model, so inference needs no reference audio.
entries.condition: Visual video features plus vision-derived speaker representation; no audio reference at inference.
entries.quote: conditioned on the channel-wise concatenation of the vision-guided speaker embeddings sv and the visual features fv

entries.text: The denoiser predicts the clean mel-spectrogram M0 rather than diffusion noise; training minimizes L1 distance to the ground-truth mel-spectrogram.
entries.value: L1 reconstruction loss on predicted versus ground-truth mel-spectrogram
entries.condition: Diffusion training conditioned on visual features and vision-guided speaker embedding.

entries.text: At sampling, a cosine-similarity speaker-embedding guidance term steers the generated mel toward the video-derived speaker identity; sampling uses deterministic DDIM with T=1000 and guidance weight λ=1000.
entries.condition: Speaker guidance compares the vision-guided video embedding with an audio-guided embedding extracted from the predicted mel; deterministic DDIM. No random seeds are stated.

entries.text: Evaluation uses the LRS2-BBC test split (1,200 utterances) and LRS3-TED test split (about 1,300 utterances); LRS3 is described as English with >50,000 vocabularies and thousands of speakers, and uses the unseen-data split. Per-test speaker counts are not given.

questions.q: What inputs does LipDiffuser require at inference, and what does it generate?
questions.answer: It uses silent lip video and an enrollment utterance for the target speaker, then generates a mel-spectrogram and synthesizes a waveform with HiFi-GAN.

questions.q: What is the paper's central architectural contribution?
questions.answer: MP-FiLM fuses time-aligned, interpolated video features into an MP-ADM denoiser on a per-frame basis while preserving activation magnitude.

questions.q: What evidence supports the authors' quality and speaker-similarity superiority claim?
questions.answer: At -10 dB on LRS3-CHiME3, Table 1 reports LipDiffuser's DNSMOS, NISQA, and SpkSim results; the authors also report a 15-participant listening experiment, though the extracted text gives no exact listening-score values.

questions.q: Does the paper claim LipDiffuser is best on ASR and phoneme similarity?
questions.answer: No. The authors describe WER and LPS as comparable to LipVoicer and IL2S (SSL), while claiming substantial gains over speech-enhancement systems.

questions.q: Which evaluation details should a reviewer treat as unspecified?
questions.answer: Exact split construction and counts, seeds and run repetitions, speaker overlap, validation/checkpoint selection, evaluation normalization, chance baselines, detailed cross-dataset conditions, and listening-study protocol details are not stated.

questions.q: Did the paper link public code that could supply omitted conditions?
questions.answer: No project-code repository is linked; the paper says code and checkpoints would be made available upon acceptance, so there are no repo scripts to inspect.
